comment: Hand-entered inputs of features-bubbles.json. Every value carries evidence { source, quote } checked against the fetched paper by bubbles.mjs. The lobe geometry is derived in bubbles.mjs from the quoted extents (see its header comment).

features.name: Fermi bubbles
features.noun: Gamma-ray lobes above and below the Galactic centre

evidence.quote: extending 50 degrees above and below the Galactic center, with a width of about 40 degrees in longitude

lobes.note: each lobe reaches from the plane to latitude 50 deg, i.e. 8178 pc × tan 50° above Sgr A* when its far edge is taken in the plane of the sky through the centre, so the lobe centre is {offset} pc above (below) Sgr A*; the 40 deg width at the lobe-centre distance gives the cross-section; the extent along the line of sight is not measured and is set equal to the width. features.description: Two giant lobes of GeV gamma rays discovered in Fermi-LAT maps, symmetric about the Galactic plane and rooted at the Galactic centre, with sharp edges and a hard spectrum. They are probably the product of a burst of activity of the central black hole or of nuclear star formation within the last ~10 Myr. Invisible to the eye: they are seen in gamma rays (and, closer to the plane, in the microwave 'haze'). Label at the centre of the northern lobe.

features.name: eROSITA bubbles
features.noun: X-ray shells above and below the Galactic centre

evidence.quote: assuming a spherical geometry, they would extend roughly 14 kpc above and below the Galactic plane

lobes.note: Predehl et al. 2020 describe each bubble as a (quasi-)spherical thick shell with an outer diameter of 14 kpc, reaching about 14 kpc above (below) the plane; each lobe is drawn as a sphere of radius 7 kpc centred {offset} pc above (below) Sgr A*. Semi-axes {axes} pc, approximate.

features.description: Two enormous shells of soft X-ray emission (0.6-1.0 keV) found in the first all-sky survey of the eROSITA telescope, about twice the size of the Fermi bubbles which they enclose; the northern one includes the long-known North Polar Spur / Loop I region. Predehl et al. 2020 interpret them as a shock driven into the Galaxy's hot halo by an energy release at the Galactic centre some tens of millions of years ago. Invisible to the eye: they are seen only in X-rays. Label at the centre of the northern lobe.
